Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $k\ge 0$. A **smooth differential $k$-form**
on $M$ is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M\to M$. The space of such forms
is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, and $\Omega^0(M)=C^\infty(M)$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $(U,x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ be a smooth chart on a smooth manifold and
$\omega$ a smooth $k$-form on $U$, with $k\ge0$. Summing over increasing
$k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$
For every differential form $\omega$, $d(d\omega)=0$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $n\ge1$.  A linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$
([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$B:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ such that

$$B(Au)=u\quad\hbox{and}\quad A(Bu)=u\qquad(u\in\mathbb R^n).$$

The map $B$ is unique: if $C$ has the same two properties, then
$C=C\circ(A\circ B)=(C\circ A)\circ B=B$.  It is denoted $A^{-1}$.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

Let $n\ge1$.  A linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$
([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$B:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ such that

$$B(Au)=u\quad\hbox{and}\quad A(Bu)=u\qquad(u\in\mathbb R^n).$$

The map $B$ is unique: if $C$ has the same two properties, then
$C=C\circ(A\circ B)=(C\circ A)\circ B=B$.  It is denoted $A^{-1}$.

A **symplectic vector space** is a pair $(V,\omega)$ consisting of a
finite-dimensional real vector space $V$ and an alternating bilinear form
$\omega:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ for which

$$\omega^\flat:V\longrightarrow V^*,\qquad \omega^\flat(v)=\omega(v,\,·),$$

is an isomorphism. Equivalently, $\omega(v,w)=0$ for every $w\in V$ implies
$v=0$. The equivalence also follows from the radical clause in
[[thm-alternating-forms-have-a-symplectic-normal-form]]. The zero vector space,
with its unique alternating form, is included: its map to its dual is the
unique isomorphism.

A **symplectic form** on a smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth two-form $\omega$
such that

1. $d\omega=0$, and
2. $(T_pM,\omega_p)$ is a [[def-symplectic-vector-space|symplectic vector
   space]] for every $p\in M$.

The pair $(M,\omega)$ is a **symplectic manifold**. Thus both closedness and
pointwise nondegeneracy are required. A zero-dimensional manifold with its
zero two-form satisfies the definition.

derivations.claim: Closedness: since $dq^i\wedge dp_i=d(q^i\,dp_i)$ by [F2], summing gives $\omega_U=d\gamma$ with $\gamma=\sum_i q^i\,dp_i$, whence $d\omega_U=d^2\gamma=0$.

Evaluation and contraction: by [F1], $\omega_z(v,w)=\sum_i(a^i d_i-c^i b_i)=a\cdot d-b\cdot c$; in block form this is $v^{\mathsf T}Jw$, since $Jw=(d,-c)$ and $(a,b)\cdot(d,-c)=a\cdot d-b\cdot c$. Reading the same evaluation as a covector in $w$ gives $\iota_v\omega_z=\sum_i a_i\,dp_i-\sum_i b_i\,dq^i$.
Block identities: [F3] gives $J^{\mathsf T}=-J$, $J^2=-I_{2n}$ and $J^{-1}=J^{\mathsf T}=-J$.

Nondegeneracy: if $\iota_v\omega_z=0$, then by step 1.2 the covector has all coefficients zero, so $a=0$ and $b=0$, that is $v=0$; hence the linear map $v\mapsto\iota_v\omega_z$ has trivial kernel and, by [F4], is an isomorphism $\mathbb R^{2n}\to(\mathbb R^{2n})^*$. Thus $\omega_z$ is nondegenerate and, with step 1.1, $(U,\omega_U)$ is a symplectic manifold.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U$ be a phase domain with canonical one-form $\lambda_U$, standard two-form
$\omega_U=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ and matrix $J=\begin{pmatrix}0_n&I_n\\-I_n&0_n\end{pmatrix}$
([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]). For a point $z\in U$ write
$\omega_z:=(\omega_U)_z$. Then:

1. $\omega_U$ is closed: $d\omega_U=0$;
2. for all $v,w\in\mathbb R^{2n}$, written in the coordinate frame as $v=(a,b)$ and $w=(c,d)$ with
   $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb R^n$, one has
   $$\omega_z(v,w)=v^{\mathsf T}J\,w=a\cdot d-b\cdot c ;$$
3. for every $v=(a,b)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n$ the contraction is the covector
   $$\iota_v\omega_z=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,dp_i-\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\,dq^i ;$$
4. $J^{\mathsf T}=-J$, $J^2=-I_{2n}$, and $J$ is invertible with $J^{-1}=J^{\mathsf T}=-J$;
5. consequently $v\mapsto\iota_v\omega_z$ is a linear isomorphism $\mathbb R^{2n}\to(\mathbb R^{2n})^*$,
   so $\omega_U$ is nondegenerate at every point and $(U,\omega_U)$ is a symplectic manifold.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with $\|r(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2\to0$.

For $H\in C^\infty(M)$, its **Hamiltonian vector field** is the vector field
$X_H$ determined by the library sign convention

$$\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH.$$

A vector field $X$ is **Hamiltonian** if $\iota_X\omega=dH$ for some smooth
function $H$; such an $H$ is a **Hamiltonian function for $X$**. A function and
its vector field are distinct data, and completeness of $X_H$ is not assumed.

For $F,G\in C^\infty(M)$, the **Poisson bracket** in the library convention is

$$\{F,G\}:=\omega(X_F,X_G)=dF(X_G)=X_G(F)=-X_F(G).$$

All four formulas use $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$. In particular, the order in the
observable formula is important: evolution by $H$ differentiates $F$ as
$X_H(F)=\{F,H\}$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, so that $TM$ carries its canonical smooth
structure. Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. A **smooth vector field** on $M$ is a
smooth section

$$ X:M\to TM $$

of the tangent-bundle projection $\pi:TM\to M$. Thus $\pi\circ X=\operatorname{id}_M$.

Equivalently, for each $p\in M$ the value $X(p)$ is a tangent vector in $T_pM$,
and the dependence on $p$ is smooth with respect to the canonical smooth
structure on $TM$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $a_0\in U$, and let $T>0$, $R>0$ with $\overline B(a_0,R)\subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). Put $M:=\sup_{\overline B(a_0,R)}\|F\|_2$ and $L:=\sup_{\overline B(a_0,R)}\|DF\|$, where $DF(x)$ is the total derivative of $F$ at $x$ with its operator norm ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]); both are finite. Let $0<\rho<R-MT$, so that in particular $MT<R$. Let $\Phi$ be the local flow of $x'=F(x)$ ([[def-cm-local-flow-of-an-autonomous-system]]).

Then:

1. For every $a\in\overline B(a_0,\rho)$ the maximal solution $x(\,\cdot\,;a)$ is defined on $[0,T]$ and satisfies $\|x(t;a)-a_0\|_2\le\rho+Mt<R$ for $t\in[0,T]$; moreover

$$\|x(t;a)-x(t;b)\|_2\le e^{Lt}\|a-b\|_2\qquad(a,b\in\overline B(a_0,\rho),\ t\in[0,T]),$$

and $(t,a)\mapsto x(t;a)$ is continuous on the compact set $[0,T]\times\overline B(a_0,\rho)$.

2. For every $a\in B(a_0,\rho)$ the variational equation along $x(\,\cdot\,;a)$,

$$Y'(t)=DF\bigl(x(t;a)\bigr)Y(t),\qquad Y(0)=I_n,$$

has a unique solution $Y_a:[0,T]\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-variational-equation-along-an-ode-solution]]), and for every $t\in[0,T]$ the map $a\mapsto x(t;a)$ is differentiable on the open ball $B(a_0,\rho)$, with

$$D_a x(t;a)h=Y_a(t)h\qquad(h\in\mathbb R^n).$$

3. The map $(t,a)\mapsto Y_a(t)$ is continuous on $[0,T]\times B(a_0,\rho)$, and consequently $(t,a)\mapsto x(t;a)$ is $C^1$ there with

$$\partial_t x(t;a)=F\bigl(x(t;a)\bigr),\qquad D_a x(t;a)=Y_a(t).$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U$ be a phase domain with standard two-form
$\omega_U=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ ([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]), and let
$H:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Write
$\nabla H=(H_{q^1},\dots,H_{q^n},H_{p_1},\dots,H_{p_n})$ for the Euclidean gradient
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) and $J$ for the standard symplectic matrix. Then:

1. there is exactly one $C^1$ vector field $X_H$ on $U$ with $\iota_{X_H}\omega_U=dH$, and it is
   $$X_H=J\nabla H=\bigl(H_{p_1},\dots,H_{p_n},-H_{q^1},\dots,-H_{q^n}\bigr);$$
2. an integral curve $t\mapsto(q(t),p(t))$ of $X_H$ satisfies Hamilton's equations
   $$\dot q^i=H_{p_i}(q,p),\qquad \dot p_i=-H_{q^i}(q,p)\qquad(i=1,\dots,n);$$
3. for $f,g\in C^2(U)$ the Poisson bracket
   $\{f,g\}:=\omega_U(X_f,X_g)$ ([[def-poisson-bracket-on-a-symplectic-manifold]]) is
   $$\{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\,\nabla g=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(f_{q^i}g_{p_i}-f_{p_i}g_{q^i}\bigr),$$
   hence $\{f,g\}=-\{g,f\}$, and $\{f,g\}$ is $C^1$ on $U$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].
For a $C^2$ scalar field $f$, $H_f(a)^T=H_f(a)$ at every point $a$.

For each fixed $n\ge1$, the function $\det:M_n(\mathbb R)\to\mathbb R$ is evaluation of the polynomial
$$P_n:=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}x_{\sigma(i),i}$$
in the $n^2$ commuting variables $x_{ri}$.

Let $f,g:X\to\mathbb R$ be continuous maps from a topological space. Then
$f+g$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max(f,g)$, and $\min(f,g)$ are continuous. On the open
cozero set $\operatorname{coz}(g)$, the quotient $f/g$ is continuous. The same
holds for every finite sum, product, maximum, or minimum of continuous
real-valued maps.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function, with images and preimages written $f[\,\cdot\,]$
and $f^{-1}[\,\cdot\,]$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). Conditions
(a), (b), (c), and (e) below are equivalent without choice, and each implies
(d). Assuming Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), all five are
equivalent. The authorized Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) suffices;
only its countable instance is used for the converse from (d).

- **(a)** $f$ is continuous at every point of $X$ in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$
  sense ([[def-metric-continuity]]).
- **(b)** $f^{-1}[V]$ is open in $X$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
  ([[def-metric-topology]]).
- **(c)** $f^{-1}[G]$ is closed in $X$ for every closed $G \subseteq Y$.
- **(d)** $f$ is **sequentially continuous**: whenever $x_k \to x$ in $(X,d_X)$,
  also $f(x_k) \to f(x)$ in $(Y,d_Y)$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]).
- **(e)** $f[\overline{A}] \subseteq \overline{f[A]}$ for every $A \subseteq X$
  ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

**Where choice is used.** Only the implication (d) $\Rightarrow$ (e) uses a
choice principle, and it uses it only through
[[thm-metric-sequential-closure]], whose forward direction spends the Axiom of
Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The cycle
(a) $\Rightarrow$ (b) $\Rightarrow$ (c) $\Rightarrow$ (e) $\Rightarrow$ (a) and
the implication (a) $\Rightarrow$ (d) are choice free.

Let $(X, d_X)$ and $(Y, d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]), let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $a \in X$.

$f$ is **continuous at $a$** if for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that

$$d_X(x,a) < \delta \;\Longrightarrow\; d_Y\big(f(x), f(a)\big) < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for all } x \in X .$$

$f$ is **continuous** (globally, or on $X$) if it is continuous at every point of
$X$.

**The same condition in balls.** Since $d_X(x,a) < \delta$ says $x \in B_X(a,\delta)$
and $d_Y(f(x),f(a)) < \varepsilon$ says $f(x) \in B_Y(f(a),\varepsilon)$
([[def-metric-ball]]), continuity at $a$ reads: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there
is $\delta > 0$ with

$$f\big[B_X(a,\delta)\big] \subseteq B_Y\big(f(a), \varepsilon\big).$$

Both forms are used below and are the same statement written twice.

**Both metrics matter, and both are named.** Continuity is a property of the
triple $(d_X, d_Y, f)$, not of $f$ alone. When several metrics on the same
underlying sets are in play, as in [[def-equivalent-metrics]], the metrics are
always written out.

**Quantifier order.** The $\delta$ is allowed to depend on $\varepsilon$ **and on
the point $a$**. Requiring one $\delta$ to work at every point simultaneously is
a strictly stronger condition, uniform continuity; it is defined on a later page
of this library, and at this point in the reading order it is written out in full
where needed ([[def-equivalent-metrics]]).

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

For every $n\ge1$, every commutative ring $R$, and every $A\in M_n(R)$,
$$\det(A^{\mathsf T})=\det(A).$$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $n\geq1$, and $A\in M_n(R)$. Then $A$ is
invertible if and only if $\det(A)$ is a unit of $R$.

Let $n\ge1$.  A linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$
([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$B:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ such that

$$B(Au)=u\quad\hbox{and}\quad A(Bu)=u\qquad(u\in\mathbb R^n).$$

The map $B$ is unique: if $C$ has the same two properties, then
$C=C\circ(A\circ B)=(C\circ A)\circ B=B$.  It is denoted $A^{-1}$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim: Clause 1: by [F1] the map $Y$ is $C^1$ on $I$ and solves $Y'=DF(\Phi_t(z_0))Y$ with $Y(0)=I_{2n}$; since $X_H=J\nabla H$ and $J$ is constant, the chain rule gives $DF(z)=J\,\mathrm{Hess}\,H(z)$, so $Y'(t)=J\,\mathrm{Hess}\,H(\Phi_t(z_0))Y(t)$.

Clause 2: put $A(t):=J\,\mathrm{Hess}\,H(\Phi_t(z_0))$. By [F2] and [F3], $A^{\mathsf T}=(\mathrm{Hess}\,H)^{\mathsf T}J^{\mathsf T}=(\mathrm{Hess}\,H)(-J)=-\mathrm{Hess}\,H\,J$ and $JA=J^2\mathrm{Hess}\,H=-\mathrm{Hess}\,H$, so $A^{\mathsf T}J+JA=-\mathrm{Hess}\,H\,JJ-\mathrm{Hess}\,H=(\mathrm{Hess}\,H)(-J^2)-\mathrm{Hess}\,H=0$; hence $\frac{d}{dt}(Y^{\mathsf T}JY)=Y'^{\mathsf T}JY+Y^{\mathsf T}JY'=Y^{\mathsf T}(A^{\mathsf T}J+JA)Y=0$, and $Y(t)^{\mathsf T}JY(t)=Y(0)^{\mathsf T}JY(0)=J$ for all $t\in I$.

Clause 3: taking determinants in clause 2 and using [F4] gives $\det(Y^{\mathsf T}JY)=\det(Y^{\mathsf T})\det(J)\det(Y)=(\det Y)^2\det J$, so $(\det Y(t))^2\det J=\det J$; since $\det J\ne0$, $(\det Y(t))^2=1$ for all $t\in I$; by [F4] the function $t\mapsto\det Y(t)$ is continuous with $\det Y(0)=\det I_{2n}=1$, so the sign rigidity [F5] gives $\det Y\equiv1$.

boundaries.reason: The base point z_0 belongs to U and the flow time interval contains zero; Y has the fixed shape 2n by 2n with n>=1, so none of these data is an empty family.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 uses d/dt to differentiate Y transpose J Y; dt is not a scalar denominator. At t=0, step 1.1 gives Y=I, fixing the invariant to J.
For n=1, the Hessian in step 2.1 is a symmetric two by two matrix and A=J Hess H still satisfies A transpose J+JA=0.
Even when Hess H is singular, step 2.1 remains valid by symmetry and uses no Hessian inverse. Step 3.1 then forces det Y=1, so the flow derivative itself is nonsingular.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and let $\Phi:\Omega\to U$ be the local flow of $x'=F(x)$ with maximal solutions $x(\,\cdot\,;a):I_a\to U$ ([[def-cm-local-flow-of-an-autonomous-system]]). Then $\Omega$ is open in $\mathbb R\times U$ ([[def-metric-topology]]), and $\Phi$ is of class $C^1$ on $\Omega$, with

$$\partial_t\Phi(t,a)=F\bigl(\Phi(t,a)\bigr)\qquad((t,a)\in\Omega).$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]. Read the autonomous system

$$x'(t)=F(x(t))$$

as the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] with domain $D=\mathbb R\times U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ and right-hand side $(t,x)\mapsto F(x)$. Its initial value problems satisfy the Picard-Lindelöf hypotheses, so by [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] every $a\in U$ has a unique maximal solution.

For $a\in U$ denote by

$$x(\,\cdot\,;a):I_a\longrightarrow U$$

the unique maximal solution with $x(0;a)=a$, where $I_a\subseteq\mathbb R$ is its maximal interval of existence ([[def-maximal-ode-solution]]); $I_a$ is an open interval containing $0$, and every solution of $x'=F(x)$ through $(0,a)$ is a restriction of $x(\,\cdot\,;a)$.

The **flow domain** of $F$ is the set

$$\Omega:=\{\,(t,a)\in\mathbb R\times U\;:\;t\in I_a\,\},$$

and the **local flow** (also **phase flow**) of $F$ is the map

$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow U,\qquad \Phi(t,a):=x(t;a).$$

For $t\in\mathbb R$ the **time-$t$ map** is the partial map

$$\Phi_t:\Omega_t\longrightarrow U,\qquad \Omega_t:=\{\,a\in U:(t,a)\in\Omega\,\},\qquad \Phi_t(a):=\Phi(t,a).$$

Thus $\Phi_0(a)=a$ whenever it is defined, and $(t,a)\in\Omega$ exactly when the maximal solution of $x'=F(x)$ through $a$ is defined at time $t$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U$ be a phase domain with standard two-form $\omega_U$ and matrix $J$, let
$H\in C^2(U)$, and let $\Phi$ be the local flow of the Hamiltonian field
$X_H=J\nabla H$ ([[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]],
[[def-cm-local-flow-of-an-autonomous-system]]). Let $z_0\in U$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be the open
interval of times $t$ with $(t,z_0)$ in the flow domain, and for $t\in I$ put

$$Y(t):=D_z\Phi_t(z_0)\in M_{2n}(\mathbb R).$$

Then $t\mapsto Y(t)$ is of class $C^1$ on $I$ and, for every $t\in I$:

1. (variational equation) $Y'(t)=J\,\mathrm{Hess}\,H(\Phi_t(z_0))\,Y(t)$ and $Y(0)=I_{2n}$;
2. (canonical matrix identity) $Y(t)^{\mathsf T}J\,Y(t)=J$;
3. (unit determinant) $\det Y(t)=1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: By [F1] the map $\Phi_t:D_t\to\Phi_t(D_t)$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism between open subsets of $\mathbb R^{2n}$, and by [F4] the set $\Phi_t(A)$ is a bounded Borel set whose indicator is integrable; moreover $|\det D\Phi_t|=1$ on $D_t$ by [F2].

Apply [F3] with $T=\Phi_t$, $V=D_t$ and $f=\mathbf 1_{\Phi_t(A)}\in L^1$: since $f\circ T=\mathbf 1_A$ and $|\det DT|=1$, the identity $\int f\,d\lambda_{2n}=\int(f\circ T)|\det DT|\,d\lambda_{2n}$ reads $\lambda_{2n}(\Phi_t(A))=\int\mathbf 1_A\,d\lambda_{2n}=\lambda_{2n}(A)$, which is the claim.

boundaries.evidence: The bounded Borel set A is allowed to be empty. Step 2.1 uses its indicator, then both integrals and both Lebesgue measures are zero; no nonempty A hypothesis is needed.
A may have zero measure while nonempty; the indicator change-of-variables computation in step 2.1 still gives lambda(Phi_t(A))=0 exactly.
For n=1, step 2.1 applies the same change-of-variables theorem on R² with determinant one, preserving planar area.

boundaries.reason: The time-t map is a C^1 diffeomorphism on D_t by step 1.1; a singular flow derivative is ruled out by the canonical matrix supplier.
The set closure A lies inside D_t. No measure claim is made across points where the partial flow ceases to exist.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement explicitly assumes Countable Choice for the change-of-variables supplier; step 2.1 is its precise use, and the former no-choice row was inaccurate.

boundaries.reason: The measure equality is the conclusion for a Hamiltonian flow under the stated choice hypothesis; it is not a criterion equivalent to being Hamiltonian.
Volume preservation alone is not claimed to imply canonicity or Hamiltonian generation; this corollary supplies only the announced equality.

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth, and let $\omega\in\Omega^k(N)$. The **pullback**
$F^*\omega$ is the pullback of $\omega$ viewed as an alternating covariant
$k$-tensor field:

$$ (F^*\omega)_p(v_1,\ldots,v_k)=\omega_{F(p)}(dF_pv_1,\ldots,dF_pv_k). $$

Let $\alpha\in\Omega^k(M)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^\ell(M)$. Their **wedge product**
is the differential form defined pointwise by

$$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM). $$

The next proposition verifies that this pointwise field is smooth.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with $\|r(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2\to0$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U$ be a phase domain with canonical one-form $\lambda_U$, standard two-form
$\omega_U=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ and matrix $J=\begin{pmatrix}0_n&I_n\\-I_n&0_n\end{pmatrix}$
([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]). For a point $z\in U$ write
$\omega_z:=(\omega_U)_z$. Then:

1. $\omega_U$ is closed: $d\omega_U=0$;
2. for all $v,w\in\mathbb R^{2n}$, written in the coordinate frame as $v=(a,b)$ and $w=(c,d)$ with
   $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb R^n$, one has
   $$\omega_z(v,w)=v^{\mathsf T}J\,w=a\cdot d-b\cdot c ;$$
3. for every $v=(a,b)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n$ the contraction is the covector
   $$\iota_v\omega_z=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,dp_i-\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\,dq^i ;$$
4. $J^{\mathsf T}=-J$, $J^2=-I_{2n}$, and $J$ is invertible with $J^{-1}=J^{\mathsf T}=-J$;
5. consequently $v\mapsto\iota_v\omega_z$ is a linear isomorphism $\mathbb R^{2n}\to(\mathbb R^{2n})^*$,
   so $\omega_U$ is nondegenerate at every point and $(U,\omega_U)$ is a symplectic manifold.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U$ be a phase domain with standard two-form
$\omega_U=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ ([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]), and let
$H:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Write
$\nabla H=(H_{q^1},\dots,H_{q^n},H_{p_1},\dots,H_{p_n})$ for the Euclidean gradient
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) and $J$ for the standard symplectic matrix. Then:

1. there is exactly one $C^1$ vector field $X_H$ on $U$ with $\iota_{X_H}\omega_U=dH$, and it is
   $$X_H=J\nabla H=\bigl(H_{p_1},\dots,H_{p_n},-H_{q^1},\dots,-H_{q^n}\bigr);$$
2. an integral curve $t\mapsto(q(t),p(t))$ of $X_H$ satisfies Hamilton's equations
   $$\dot q^i=H_{p_i}(q,p),\qquad \dot p_i=-H_{q^i}(q,p)\qquad(i=1,\dots,n);$$
3. for $f,g\in C^2(U)$ the Poisson bracket
   $\{f,g\}:=\omega_U(X_f,X_g)$ ([[def-poisson-bracket-on-a-symplectic-manifold]]) is
   $$\{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\,\nabla g=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(f_{q^i}g_{p_i}-f_{p_i}g_{q^i}\bigr),$$
   hence $\{f,g\}=-\{g,f\}$, and $\{f,g\}$ is $C^1$ on $U$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

$k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$
For every differential form $\omega$, $d(d\omega)=0$.

For the complex [[def-de-rham-cochain-complex]], put $Z^k(M)=\ker(d:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{k+1}(M))$ and $B^k(M)=\operatorname{im}(d:\Omega^{k-1}(M)\to\Omega^k(M))$. A form is **closed** if it belongs to $Z^k$ and **exact** if it belongs to $B^k$.

If $\omega=d\eta$, then $d\omega=d^2\eta=0$ by [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-squares-to-zero]], so $B^k\subseteq Z^k$. In particular $B^0=0$, since $\Omega^{-1}=0$. The zero form is both closed and exact in every degree.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], $F:W\to W''$ is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism with $C^2$ inverse $G$; on $W''$ the functions $p_i:=p_i\circ G$ and $P_i:=P_i\circ G$ are $C^2$ in $(q,Q)$.

Define the $C^2$ one-form $\alpha:=\sum_i p_i\,dq^i-\sum_i P_i\,dQ^i$ on $W''$, with the functions of step 1.1. Its exterior derivative is $d\alpha=\sum_i dp_i\wedge dq^i-\sum_i dP_i\wedge dQ^i =\sum_i dQ^i\wedge dP_i-\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ (using $dp\wedge dq=-dq\wedge dp$ and $dP\wedge dQ=-dQ\wedge dP$); by [F3] this vanishes, so $\alpha$ is closed ([[def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms]]).

The ball $W''$ is open and star-shaped about its centre $F(z_0)$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]], [[def-metric-topology]]), and the one-form $\alpha$ of step 2.1 is a closed $C^1$ one-form on it (indeed $C^2$); by [F4] there is a $C^3$ function $S:W''\to\mathbb R$ with $dS=\alpha$, that is, $S_{q^i}=p_i$ and $S_{Q^j}=-P_j$.

At $F(z_0)$ one has $\det S_{qQ}=\det(\partial p_i/\partial Q^j)$; since $DG$ is the inverse of $DF$ and $DG$ has block form $\begin{pmatrix}I_n&0\cr \partial p/\partial q&\partial p/\partial Q \end{pmatrix}$, the identity $DG\,DF=I_{2n}$ gives $(\partial p/\partial Q)(z_0)\,(Q_p(z_0))=I_n$; by [F1] the factor $Q_p(z_0)$ is invertible, hence $\det S_{qQ}(F(z_0))\ne0$.

By [F5] the function $S$ is a first-kind generating function on a neighbourhood of $F(z_0)$; the relations $p=S_q$, $P=-S_Q$ of step 3.1 are exactly the defining relations of the map generated by $S$ ([[def-cm-generating-function-of-the-first-and-second-kind]]), and they hold on the image of $C$ under the identification $F$; hence the generated local map agrees with $C$ near $z_0$.

boundaries.reason: The hypothesis supplies z_0 in U and the proof ball W double-prime contains F(z_0) in step 1.1. The finite coordinate one-form in step 2.1 therefore has a nonempty local domain.

boundaries.evidence: A zero value of the one-form at some point causes no failure: step 3.1 uses its radial primitive rather than dividing by a coefficient p_i or P_i.

boundaries.reason: Invertibility of DF(z_0) is explicit. Step 4.1 derives the nonzero mixed determinant required for the first-kind generating function; singular projections are excluded.

$$C^*\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^n dQ^i\wedge dP_i\Bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^n dq^i\wedge dp_i .$$

([[prop-cm-canonical-map-tests-and-hamiltonian-transport]]).

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

([[def-metric-topology]]). Let $S:O_q\times O_Q\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^3$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) and assume

$$\det S_{qQ}(q,Q)\ne0\qquad\bigl((q,Q)\in O_q\times O_Q\bigr),$$

where $S_{qQ}(q,Q)$ is the $n\times n$ matrix with entries
$\partial^2 S/\partial q^i\partial Q^j(q,Q)$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]). Identify $O_q\times O_Q$ with the phase-domain coordinates
$(q,Q)$ of $\mathbb R^{2n}$ ([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]) and form the
$C^2$ map

$$\Psi:O_q\times O_Q\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{2n},\qquad \Psi(q,Q):=\bigl(q,\ S_q(q,Q)\bigr),$$

whose derivative is the block matrix
$D\Psi(q,Q)=\begin{pmatrix}I_n&0\\ S_{qq}(q,Q)&S_{qQ}(q,Q)\end{pmatrix}$. A **generating function of
the first kind** is such an $S$; the **local map generated by $S$** is, on a neighbourhood of a point
$(q_*,Q_*)$, the $C^2$ map $C:(q,p)\mapsto(Q,P)$ defined by

$$p:=S_q(q,Q),\qquad P:=-S_Q(q,Q),$$

solved as follows: since $\det S_{qQ}\ne0$, the inverse function theorem
([[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]) makes $\Psi$ a local $C^2$ diffeomorphism, so
$p=S_q(q,Q)$ determines a $C^2$ local inverse $Q=Q(q,p)$ on a neighbourhood of

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

derivations.claim: Clause 1: by [F2] and [F1], $\pi^*(\Phi^*\omega_C)=(\Phi\circ\pi)^*\omega_C=(\pi\circ\tilde\Phi)^*\omega_C=\tilde\Phi^*(\pi^*\omega_C)=\tilde\Phi^*(d\theta\wedge dI)=d\theta\wedge dI=\pi^*\omega_C$, so injectivity of $\pi^*$ gives $\Phi^*\omega_C=\omega_C$; likewise $\pi^*(\Phi^*\lambda_C)=\tilde\Phi^*(I\,d\theta)=(I+a)\,d\theta=I\,d\theta+a\,d\theta=\pi^*(\lambda_C+a\,d\theta_C)$, which gives $\Phi^*\lambda_C=\lambda_C+a\,d\theta_C$.
Clause 2, closedness: $d(a\,d\theta_C)=a\,d(d\theta_C)=0$ because $\pi^*(d(d\theta_C))=d(d\theta)=0$ and $\pi^*$ is injective; so $a\,d\theta_C$ is closed.

Clause 2, non-exactness: suppose $W:C\to\mathbb R$ is $C^1$ with $dW=a\,d\theta_C$, and set $g(t):=W(\pi(t,0))$ for $t\in[0,1]$. By the chain rule and $d\theta_C(\partial_\theta)=1$ at the image point, $g$ is $C^1$ with $g'(t)=a$ for $0<t<1$; by [F3], $g(1)-g(0)=a$. But $\pi(1,0)=\pi(0,0)$ in $C$, so $g(1)=g(0)$; this contradicts $a\ne0$. Hence no such $W$ exists, and $\Phi^*\lambda_C-\lambda_C=a\,d\theta_C$ is a closed form representing a nonzero class.

Clause 3, global failure: suppose a $C^1$ function $S$ exists on $(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)\times\mathbb R$ whose generated second-kind map is $\Phi$, that is, with $p=S_\theta=I=P-a$ and $Q=S_P$ equal to the circle coordinate $\theta$ at every point, the former because $\Phi$ carries $(\theta,I)$ to $(\theta,I+a)$, so the new momentum is $P=I+a$ and the old momentum is $I=P-a$. Lift $S$ to a $1$-periodic $C^1$ function $\hat S$ on $\mathbb R^2$. The relation $Q=\theta$ reads $\hat S_P(\theta,P)-\theta\in\mathbb Z$; since this difference is continuous and integer-valued on $\mathbb R^2$, it is constant: if it took two distinct values, the intermediate value theorem applied along the segment joining the corresponding points would produce a non-integer value. Write the constant as $m\in\mathbb Z$, so $\hat S_P(\theta,P)=\theta+m$; the fundamental theorem of calculus in $P$ gives $\hat S(\theta,P)=\theta P+mP+c(\theta)$ with $c(\theta):=\hat S(\theta,0)$. Differentiating in $\theta$ gives $\hat S_\theta(\theta,P)=P+c'(\theta)=P-a$, so $c'(\theta)=-a$ and, by [F3] in the variable $\theta$, $c(1)-c(0)=-a\ne0$, contradicting the $1$-periodicity $c(1)=c(0)$ of the lift. Hence no global $S$ exists, while [F4] exhibits the local generating function $S(\theta,P)=\theta P-a\theta$ on every chart where $\theta$ is a single-valued coordinate.

Let $n\ge1$, let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval
([[def-interval]]), let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty open set, and let

$$H:J\times U\times\mathbb R^n\longrightarrow\mathbb R$$

be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); write $p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ for
the third variable, so that $(t,q,p)$ range over phase-type data and $H$ is a Hamiltonian in the
sense of [[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]]. Let
$J'\subseteq J$, $U'\subseteq U$ and $A'\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty open sets
([[def-metric-topology]]) and let $S:J'\times U'\times A'\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^3$; write
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ for the third variable.

$S$ **solves the Hamilton-Jacobi equation associated with $H$** on $J'\times U'\times A'$ if

$$S_t(t,q,\alpha)+H\bigl(t,\,q,\,S_q(t,q,\alpha)\bigr)=0\qquad\bigl((t,q,\alpha)\in J'\times U'\times A'\bigr),$$

where $S_t$ is the partial derivative in $t$, $S_q=(S_{q^1},\dots,S_{q^n})$ is the gradient in $q$
and $H$ is evaluated at the momentum $p=S_q(t,q,\alpha)$
([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]). $S$ is a
**complete integral** of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation at $(t_0,q_0,\alpha_0)$ if in addition

$$\det S_{q\alpha}(t_0,q_0,\alpha_0)\ne0,$$

where $S_{q\alpha}$ is the $n\times n$ matrix with entries
$\partial^2S/\partial q^i\partial\alpha_j$, called the **mixed derivative**.

If $S$ is a complete integral, the associated **momentum map** is
$p(t,q,\alpha):=S_q(t,q,\alpha)$ and the associated **constants**
$\beta(t,q,\alpha):=S_\alpha(t,q,\alpha)$ are the **Jacobi constants** of the complete integral.
This is the Hamiltonian case of the general first-order equation $u_t+H(t,q,D_qu)=0$: the $n$
parameters $\alpha$ enter essentially through the nonvanishing mixed derivative, and $S_t$ is
determined algebraically by $S_q$ on the solutions.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $(U,x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ be a smooth chart on a smooth manifold and
$\omega$ a smooth $k$-form on $U$, with $k\ge0$. Summing over increasing
$k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$
For every differential form $\omega$, $d(d\omega)=0$.
For a $C^2$ scalar field $f$, $H_f(a)^T=H_f(a)$ at every point $a$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

For every $n\ge1$, every commutative ring $R$, and every $A\in M_n(R)$,
$$\det(A^{\mathsf T})=\det(A).$$

Let $n\ge1$.  A linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$
([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$B:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ such that

$$B(Au)=u\quad\hbox{and}\quad A(Bu)=u\qquad(u\in\mathbb R^n).$$

The map $B$ is unique: if $C$ has the same two properties, then
$C=C\circ(A\circ B)=(C\circ A)\circ B=B$.  It is denoted $A^{-1}$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

derivations.claim: Clause 1: by [F2] take the local solution $q$ of the characteristic equation and set $p:=S_q(t,q,\alpha)$. Then $p'(t)=S_{tq}+S_{qq}q'$ by the chain rule; differentiating the Hamilton-Jacobi equation in $q$ gives $S_{tq}+H_q+H_pS_{qq}=0$ at $(t,q(t),\alpha)$; substituting $q'=H_p$ and using the symmetry of $S_{qq}$ from [F3] yields $p'=S_{tq}+S_{qq}H_p=-H_q$, while $q'=H_p$ holds by construction. Hence $(q,p)$ solves Hamilton's equations on $I_\alpha$.

Clause 4: from $dS=S_t\,dt+S_q\,dq+S_\alpha\,d\alpha=-H\,dt+p\,dq+\beta\,d\alpha$ and [F3], applying $d$ gives $0=dp\wedge dq+d\beta\wedge d\alpha-dH\wedge dt$ on $J\times U\times A$; pulling back along the inclusion of a time slice $\{t\}\times U\times A$ kills the $dt$ terms and yields $dq\wedge dp=d\beta\wedge d\alpha$ as forms on $U\times A$ at fixed $t$. By [F4] both $(q,\alpha)\mapsto(q,p)$ and $(q,\alpha)\mapsto(\beta,\alpha)$ are local diffeomorphisms (block triangular with invertible mixed block), so the composite $(q,p)\mapsto(\beta,\alpha)$ is a local diffeomorphism whose pullback of $d\beta\wedge d\alpha$ equals $dq\wedge dp$: $(\beta,\alpha)$ are local canonical coordinates.

Clause 2: by the chain rule, $\frac{d}{dt}S_{\alpha_j}=S_{\alpha_jt}+\sum_iS_{\alpha_jq_i}q'_i =S_{t\alpha_j}+\sum_iH_{p_i}S_{q_i\alpha_j}$; differentiating the Hamilton-Jacobi equation in $\alpha_j$ gives exactly $S_{t\alpha_j}+\sum_iH_{p_i}S_{q_i\alpha_j}=0$, so $\frac{d}{dt}S_{\alpha_j}=0$ and $S_\alpha$ is constant on $I_\alpha$.

Clause 3: by [F4], solve $\beta=S_\alpha(t,q,\alpha)$ locally as $q=Q(t,\alpha,\beta)$ near $(t_0,\alpha_0,\beta_0)$. Differentiating the identity $S_\alpha(t,Q,\alpha)=\beta$ in $t$ gives $S_{\alpha t}+S_{\alpha q}Q'=0$; differentiating the Hamilton-Jacobi equation in $\alpha$ gives $S_{\alpha t}+S_{\alpha q}H_p=0$; subtracting, $S_{\alpha q}(Q'-H_p)=0$, and $\det S_{\alpha q}\ne0$ gives $Q'=H_p$. With $p:=S_q(t,Q,\alpha)$, the computation of step 1.1 (which uses only $q'=H_p$ and the $q$-derivative of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation) gives $p'=-H_q$.

Clauses 1-4 are established; in particular a complete integral produces solutions of Hamilton's equations through its characteristics, its $\alpha$-derivatives are constants of those solutions, and its constants furnish local canonical coordinates.

boundaries.reason: J,U,A are explicitly nonempty and the base point (t_0,q_0,alpha_0) is given. The coordinate sums in step 2.1 use the fixed n>=1 variables.

boundaries.evidence: The derivative notation d/dt in step 2.1 is not division by a scalar dt. Vanishing momentum or a zero Jacobi constant is permitted because their values are never inverted.
With n=1, step 2.2 solves the scalar equation beta=S_alpha using nonzero S_alphaq; step 1.2 yields dq wedge dp=d beta wedge d alpha.

Characteristic curves are on open intervals containing t_0; the theorem does not claim continuation to a finite boundary of those local branches.
The local characteristic is uniquely obtained by the C^1 ODE supplier in step 1.1, and the label inversion in step 2.2 is local; no arbitrary family selection is needed.
The four clauses construct characteristics, constants and local canonical labels, including a separate local converse clause; they do not state a top-level biconditional.

citations.quote: Every closed smooth $k$-form on a star-shaped open domain is exact for $k\ge1$. For centre $0$, one primitive is $\eta_x(v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1})=\int_0^1t^{k-1}\omega_{tx}(x,v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1})\,dt$.

Let $a<b$ and $c<d$. Suppose $g,h:[a,b]\times[c,d]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and, for every fixed $t\in[c,d]$, the function $x\mapsto g(x,t)$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative $h(x,t)$. Define

$$G(x):=\int_c^d g(x,t)\,dt.$$

Then $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ as a function on that interval and

$$G'(x)=\int_c^d h(x,t)\,dt\qquad(x\in[a,b]).$$

At $a$ and $b$ the derivative is relative and one-sided. The derivative hypothesis is imposed only for interior parameter values; continuity of $h$ supplies its endpoint values.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $(U,x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ be a smooth chart on a smooth manifold and
$\omega$ a smooth $k$-form on $U$, with $k\ge0$. Summing over increasing
$k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$

derivations.claim: Specialise [F1] to $k=2$ and $\omega=\tau$: since $\tau$ is a smooth closed two-form on the star-shaped domain $U$ with centre $0$, it is exact and the one-form $\eta_x(v)=\int_0^1 t\,\tau_{tx}(x,v)\,dt$ is a smooth primitive with $d\eta=\tau$; this $\eta$ is the displayed $\alpha$, so the claim holds.

Independent coefficient verification of the display: fix a compact ball $\overline B(0,R)$ inside $U$; on the rectangle $\overline B(0,R)\times[0,1]$ the integrand $(x,t)\mapsto t\,\tau_{tx}(x,\cdot)$ and its $x$-derivatives are continuous, so [F2], applied to the one-variable functions $s\mapsto x+s\,e_k$ along the coordinate directions $e_k$, permits differentiation under the integral sign in every partial derivative, and $\partial_k\alpha_i(x)-\partial_i\alpha_k(x)=\int_0^1\bigl[2t\,\tau_{ki}(tx)+t^2\sum_j x^j(\partial_k\tau_{ji}-\partial_i\tau_{jk})(tx)\bigr]dt$. Closedness of $\tau$ reads $\partial_k\tau_{ji}+\partial_j\tau_{ik}+\partial_i\tau_{kj}=0$, which with $\tau_{kj}=-\tau_{jk}$ gives $\partial_k\tau_{ji}-\partial_i\tau_{jk}=\partial_j\tau_{ki}$; hence the bracket equals $2t\,\tau_{ki}(tx)+t^2\frac{d}{dt}\tau_{ki}(tx)=\frac{d}{dt}\bigl[t^2\tau_{ki}(tx)\bigr]$ by [F4], and [F3] gives $\partial_k\alpha_i(x)-\partial_i\alpha_k(x)=\tau_{ki}(x)$; by [F4] this says $d\alpha=\tau$.

By step 1.1 the displayed $\alpha$ is a smooth one-form with $d\alpha=\tau$, and step 1.2 confirms the same identity coefficientwise for that explicit formula; both conclusions agree, so $\alpha$ is a smooth primitive of $\tau$ on $U$.

boundaries.evidence: For n=1 the coefficient family i<j is empty, so tau=0 and alpha=0. For n>=2 the coordinate sums are fixed finite sums; step 1.1 also includes the zero two-form.
At x=0, the explicit integral alpha_x(v)=integral t tau_tx(x,v) is zero by bilinearity. The apparent d/dt in the coefficient verification of step 1.2 is differentiation, not scalar division.
Step 1.1 specializes the radial homotopy to a two-form; when n=1 every alternating two-form vanishes, so the displayed primitive and its derivative are zero.
The lemma permits tau=0 and all other rank-degenerate closed two-forms; exactness is provided by the radial homotopy in step 1.1 without a nondegeneracy hypothesis.
Step 1.2 verifies the homotopy integral on [0,1]: the t=0 endpoint is regular with prefactor zero and t=1 evaluates the coefficient at x; the radial formula in step 1.1 applies on the full interval.

boundaries.reason: The origin is the specified star center and alpha is explicitly defined by its radial integral; a primitive is not chosen separately for each form.
The claim provides a primitive for any given closed two-form on this star-shaped domain, without a top-level biconditional assertion.
No converse about arbitrary domains is asserted. The identity d alpha=tau in step 1.1 belongs to the stated radial construction on U.

citations.quote:
On a $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold, a Hamiltonian system is
**completely integrable** if it has smooth functions
$F_1=H,F_2,\ldots,F_n$ such that

1. $\{F_i,F_j\}=0$ for every $i,j$; and
2. $dF_1,\ldots,dF_n$ are linearly independent on a dense open subset.

The map $F=(F_1,\ldots,F_n):M\to\mathbb R^n$ is the **integral map**.
The set on which $dF$ has rank $n$ is its **regular locus**; it is open and,
by the preceding condition, dense.
Both involution and independence are essential. Results about regular fibres
apply only at regular values or specified regular components.

A smooth function $F$ is a **first integral** of a Hamiltonian $H$ if $F$ is
constant along every integral curve of $X_H$, on that curve's local maximal
domain. Functions $F_1,\ldots,F_k$ **Poisson commute** or are **in involution**
if $\{F_i,F_j\}=0$ for all $i,j$. The first definition does not presume that
the Hamiltonian flow is complete.

For $H\in C^\infty(M)$, its **Hamiltonian vector field** is the vector field
$X_H$ determined by the library sign convention

$$\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH.$$

A vector field $X$ is **Hamiltonian** if $\iota_X\omega=dH$ for some smooth
function $H$; such an $H$ is a **Hamiltonian function for $X$**. A function and
its vector field are distinct data, and completeness of $X_H$ is not assumed.

For every $H\in C^\infty(M)$ on a symplectic manifold $(M,\omega)$, there is
a unique smooth vector field $X_H$ satisfying $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$.

Let $(M,\omega)$ be symplectic and let $i:S\hookrightarrow M$ be a smooth
embedded submanifold of constant dimension. It is **isotropic**,
**coisotropic**, **symplectic**, or **Lagrangian** when $T_pS$ has the
corresponding property from
[[def-isotropic-coisotropic-symplectic-and-lagrangian-subspaces]] inside the
symplectic vector space $(T_pM,\omega_p)$ for every $p\in S$. Equivalently,
the symplectic case says $i^*\omega$ is nondegenerate, while the Lagrangian
case says $T_pS=(T_pS)^\omega$ at every point.

On the regular locus of a completely integrable system, the fields
$X_{F_1},\ldots,X_{F_n}$ integrate to a local $\mathbb R^n$-action. On a
compact invariant regular fibre their restrictions are complete, so the action
is global on that fibre.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Every smooth vector field on a compact manifold is complete.

This item assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, namely [[def-countable-choice|countable choice]]. In the propagated dependency chain, that assumption is required through [[cor-every-smooth-vector-field-on-a-compact-manifold-is-complete]]; after those interfaces are fixed, the remaining local or finite argument makes no additional countable-family choice.

On a compact connected regular fibre $N$ of a completely integrable system,
the $\mathbb R^n$-action is transitive. Its stabilizer $\Gamma$ is a discrete
full lattice in $\mathbb R^n$, and $N\cong\mathbb R^n/\Gamma$.

This item assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, namely [[def-countable-choice|countable choice]]. In the propagated dependency chain, that assumption is required through [[lem-stabilizer-of-the-r-n-action-on-a-compact-connected-regular-fibre-is-a-full-lattice]]; after those interfaces are fixed, the remaining local or finite argument makes no additional countable-family choice.

Every compact connected regular fibre of a completely integrable system on a
$2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold is diffeomorphic to the torus
$T^n=\mathbb R^n/\mathbb Z^n$.
For every vector field $X$ and differential form $\omega$, $$\mathcal L_X\omega=d(\iota_X\omega)+\iota_X(d\omega).$$
If $\Phi_{t,s}$ is the local evolution of $X_t$ and $\omega_t$ is a smooth time-dependent form, then $$\frac d{dt}\Phi_{t,s}^*\omega_t=\Phi_{t,s}^*(\dot\omega_t+\mathcal L_{X_t}\omega_t).$$

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$.

A **local flow** of $X$ consists of an open set $\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R\times M$
containing $\{0\}\times M$ and a smooth map $\Phi:\mathcal D\to M$ such that:

1. $\Phi(0,p)=p$ for every $p\in M$;
2. for each $p$, the fibre $\mathcal D_p:=\{t:(t,p)\in\mathcal D\}$ is an
   interval;
3. for each $p$, the curve $t\mapsto \Phi(t,p)$ is an integral curve of $X$ on
   $\mathcal D_p$;
4. whenever both sides are defined,
   $\Phi(t,\Phi(s,p))=\Phi(t+s,p)$.

If $\mathcal D=\mathbb R\times M$, then $\Phi$ is the **global flow** of $X$.

Let $F:M^m\to N^n$ be a smooth submersion at $p\in M$. Then there are charts
near $p$ and $F(p)$ in which the coordinate representative of $F$ is

$$ (u,v)\longmapsto u $$

near the distinguished point.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and star-shaped with respect to $a\in U$. Every closed $C^1$ field $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is exact. A $C^2$ potential is

$$\phi(x):=\int_0^1\left\langle F(a+t(x-a)),x-a\right\rangle\,dt.$$

A nonempty open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is **star-shaped with respect to** $a\in U$ when

$$a+t(x-a)\in U\qquad\text{for every }x\in U\text{ and }0\le t\le1.$$

The point $a$ is a **star centre**. Every convex open set of [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]] is star-shaped with respect to each of its points. The nonemptiness and the chosen centre are part of the definition.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be an open set star-shaped with respect to $0$
([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), and let $\tau$ be a smooth closed two-form on $U$
([[def-smooth-differential-k-form]], [[def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms]]). Write
$\tau=\sum_{i<j}\tau_{ij}\,dx^i\wedge dx^j$ with smooth coefficient functions $\tau_{ij}$, and extend
the coefficients by $\tau_{ji}:=-\tau_{ij}$ and $\tau_{ii}:=0$. Define
$\alpha:U\to(\mathbb R^n)^*$ by

$$\alpha_x(v):=\int_0^1 t\,\tau_{tx}(x,v)\,dt .$$

Then $\alpha$ is a smooth one-form on $U$, in coordinates

$$\alpha=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\,dx^i,\qquad \alpha_i(x)=\int_0^1 t\sum_{j=1}^n x^j\,\tau_{ji}(tx)\,dt ,$$

and $d\alpha=\tau$ on $U$. In particular every smooth closed two-form on a star-shaped
open subset of $\mathbb R^n$ is exact, with the displayed explicit primitive.

A **symplectic form** on a smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth two-form $\omega$
such that

1. $d\omega=0$, and
2. $(T_pM,\omega_p)$ is a [[def-symplectic-vector-space|symplectic vector
   space]] for every $p\in M$.

The pair $(M,\omega)$ is a **symplectic manifold**. Thus both closedness and
pointwise nondegeneracy are required. A zero-dimensional manifold with its
zero two-form satisfies the definition.

Let $n\ge1$. A **phase domain** is a nonempty open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$
([[def-metric-topology]]). Its points are written $z=(q,p)$ with
$q=(q^1,\dots,q^n)\in\mathbb R^n$ and $p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)\in\mathbb R^n$; the coordinate functions
$q^i,p_i:U\to\mathbb R$ are smooth ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and
$\partial_{q^1},\dots,\partial_{q^n},\partial_{p_1},\dots,\partial_{p_n}$ is the coordinate frame
([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). On a phase domain:

1. the **canonical one-form** is the smooth one-form
   $\lambda_U:=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\,dq^i\in\Omega^1(U)$;
2. the **standard symplectic two-form** is the smooth two-form
   $\omega_U:=\sum_{i=1}^n dq^i\wedge dp_i\in\Omega^2(U)$
   ([[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]);
3. the **standard symplectic matrix** is the block matrix
   $$J:=\begin{pmatrix}0_n&I_n\\-I_n&0_n\end{pmatrix}\in M_{2n}(\mathbb R),$$
   whose blocks are $n\times n$.

The identity $\omega_U=-d\lambda_U$ holds, because the coordinate formula for the exterior
derivative ([[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]]) gives
$d\lambda_U=\sum_i dp_i\wedge dq^i=-\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$. When $U$ is an induced chart domain of a
cotangent bundle, the published [[def-tautological-one-form-on-a-cotangent-bundle]] identifies
$\lambda_U$ and $\omega_U$ with the tautological one-form and the canonical cotangent two-form in
those coordinates; the present definition is the choice-free local coordinate model that the
canonical-calculus items of this page use.

derivations.claim: Vertical fields and the fibrewise action: for $\alpha\in\Omega^1(B)$ define the smooth field $X_\alpha$ on $U$ by $\iota_{X_\alpha}\omega=\pi^*\alpha$, which exists uniquely by [F8]; writing $\alpha=\sum_i\alpha_i\,dF_i$ with $C^\infty$ coefficients $\alpha_i$ (the $F_i$ are the coordinate functions of the ball $B$), the uniqueness in [F1] gives $X_\alpha=\sum_i\alpha_iX_{F_i}$; by [F2] the fields $X_{F_i}$ are tangent to every fibre, and for $m\in\pi^{-1}(b)$ the evaluation map $T_b^*B\to T_m\pi^{-1}(b)$, $\alpha_b\mapsto X_{\alpha_b}(m)$, is a linear isomorphism: it is injective because $\pi^*\alpha_b=0$ at $m$ forces $\alpha_b=0$ ($d\pi_m$ is surjective, $\pi$ being a submersion), and both spaces have dimension $n$. By [F3] the restricted fields are complete on every compact fibre, so their commuting flows combine into a global $\mathbb R^n$-action on each fibre, and by [F4] and [F2] each fibre $\pi^{-1}(b)$ is a single transitive orbit with stabilizer a full lattice.

The action map: shrink $B$ if necessary so that there is a smooth section $\sigma:B\to U$ through a point of $N$ ([F6]; a local section exists by the local projection form and can be restricted to a smaller ball). Define the smooth map $a:T^*B\to U$, $a(\alpha_b):=\Phi^1_{\alpha_b}(\sigma(b))$, the time-one flow of the vertical field $X_{\alpha_b}$ starting at $\sigma(b)$; it is defined because the flow preserves the compact fibre $\pi^{-1}(b)$ (step 1.1) and the restricted field is complete there. Then $Da(\alpha_b)$ is invertible for every $\alpha_b$: the base component of $Da$ is the identity because $\pi\circ a=\pi$ pointwise, and the vertical component at $\alpha_b$ is the derivative in $s$ at $s=0$ of $\Phi^1_{\alpha_b+s\beta_b}(\sigma(b))$, which by commutativity of the flows equals $X_{\beta_b}(a(\alpha_b))$; the map $T_b^*B\to T_{a(\alpha_b)}\pi^{-1}(b)$, $\beta_b\mapsto X_{\beta_b}(a(\alpha_b))$, is the isomorphism of step 1.1, so the vertical component is an isomorphism and hence by [F6] $a$ is a local diffeomorphism.

The period structure: put $\Lambda:=a^{-1}(\sigma(B))$; near each of its points $\Lambda$ is an $n$-dimensional smooth submanifold of $T^*B$ because $a$ is a local diffeomorphism there and $\sigma(B)$ is a smooth submanifold ([F6]); moreover, since $\pi\circ a=\pi$, the projection $\pi|_\Lambda$ has invertible differential, so $\Lambda$ is locally the graph of a smooth section of $T^*B\to B$. The fibre $\Lambda_{b_0}$ is the stabilizer of the point $\sigma(b_0)$ of the $\mathbb R^n$-action of step 1.1, hence by [F4] a full lattice in the fibre $T^*_{b_0}B$; choose a $\mathbb Z$-basis $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ of it, extend each to a smooth local sheet $\beta_i$ of $\Lambda$ near $b_0$, and shrink $B$ so that all $\beta_i:B\to T^*B$ are defined, are sections of $\Lambda$, and their values stay linearly independent.

A Lagrangian section: the pullback $\tau:=\sigma^*\omega$ is a smooth closed two-form on $B$ (closed because $d\tau=\sigma^*d\omega=0$); shrink $B$ to a metric ball, which is star-shaped, and by [F7] applied to the two-form $\tau$ choose a smooth one-form $\alpha$ on this ball with $d\alpha=\tau$. Define the translated section $\sigma':=\Phi^1_{-\alpha}\circ\sigma$. Then by [F5], $(\Phi^1_{-\alpha})^*\omega=\omega+\pi^*d(-\alpha)=\omega-\pi^*d\alpha$, so $(\sigma')^*\omega=\sigma^*(\Phi^1_{-\alpha})^*\omega=\tau-d(\sigma^*\pi^*\alpha)=\tau-d\alpha=0$, where $\sigma^*\pi^*\alpha=\alpha$; hence $\sigma'$ is a Lagrangian section.

Full local generation: after possibly shrinking $B$ further, for every $b\in B$ one has $\Lambda_b=\sum_i\mathbb Z\,\beta_i(b)$. Indeed, otherwise there would be, for every radius $1/r$ about $b_0$, a point $b_r$ and a period $\gamma_r\in\Lambda_{b_r}$ not in $\sum_i\mathbb Z\beta_i(b_r)$; using $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ to select the pairs $(b_r,\gamma_r)$ one may subtract the nearest integer combination of the $\beta_i(b_r)$ to arrange $\gamma_r$ in the fundamental parallelepiped of the basis $\beta_1(b_r),\dots,\beta_n(b_r)$; compactness of that parallelepiped gives a convergent subsequence, whose limit $\gamma_0$ lies in $\Lambda_{b_0}$ by continuity of $a$ and $a(\gamma_r)=\sigma(b_r)\to\sigma(b_0)$; write $\gamma_0=\sum_im_i\beta_i(b_0)$ and set $\delta_r:=\gamma_r-\sum_im_i\beta_i(b_r)\in\Lambda_{b_r}$; then $\delta_r\ne0$ by construction and $\delta_r\to0$, while $a(\delta_r)=\sigma(b_r)=a(0_{b_r})$ and both arguments eventually lie in a neighbourhood of $0_{b_0}$ on which $a$ is injective (step 2.1), a contradiction.

The sheets are closed: for each $i$, the time-one flow $\Phi^1_{\beta_i}$ of $X_{\beta_i}$ acts as the identity on every fibre, because $\beta_i(b)\in\Lambda_b$ is in the stabilizer of every point of the transitive abelian action on $\pi^{-1}(b)$ (step 4.1); hence $(\Phi^1_{\beta_i})^*\omega=\omega$; on the other hand, by [F5] and $\iota_{X_{\beta_i}}\omega=\pi^*\beta_i$, one has $\frac{d}{dt}(\Phi^t_{\beta_i})^*\omega=(\Phi^t_{\beta_i})^*d\pi^*\beta_i=\pi^*d\beta_i$, so $\omega=(\Phi^1_{\beta_i})^*\omega=\omega+\pi^*d\beta_i$ and $\pi^*d\beta_i=0$; since $\pi$ is a submersion, $\pi^*$ is injective on forms and $d\beta_i=0$.

Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

**Action–angle coordinates** on a neighbourhood $U$ fibred by Lagrangian
tori are a diffeomorphism

$$ (I,\theta):U\longrightarrow B\times(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n,$$

where $B\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is open, such that the components
$I=(I_1,\ldots,I_n)$ and
$\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)$ have fibres $I=\mathrm{constant}$ and

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\theta_i\wedge dI_i.$$

This page uses period one for every angle. Replacing angles by period $2\pi$
rescales the corresponding actions and formulas. The order
$d\theta_i\wedge dI_i$ is forced by the library convention
$\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$: it gives $\dot\theta_i=\partial H/\partial I_i$.

nonempty compact connected regular fibre. Assume that, after restricting to a saturated
neighbourhood $U$ of $N$ and a ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of regular values with $F(U)=B$, the map

$(I,\theta):U\to B'\times T^n$ in the sense of [[def-action-and-angle-coordinates]] (period-one

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\theta_i\wedge dI_i ,$$

and every $C^\infty$ function on $U$ that is constant on the fibres of $\pi$ (in particular each
$F_i$) is a function of $I$ alone.

Let $n\ge1$. A **phase domain** is a nonempty open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$
([[def-metric-topology]]). Its points are written $z=(q,p)$ with
$q=(q^1,\dots,q^n)\in\mathbb R^n$ and $p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)\in\mathbb R^n$; the coordinate functions

$\partial_{q^1},\dots,\partial_{q^n},\partial_{p_1},\dots,\partial_{p_n}$ is the coordinate frame

   $\lambda_U:=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\,dq^i\in\Omega^1(U)$;
2. the **standard symplectic two-form** is the smooth two-form
   $\omega_U:=\sum_{i=1}^n dq^i\wedge dp_i\in\Omega^2(U)$
   ([[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]);
3. the **standard symplectic matrix** is the block matrix
   $$J:=\begin{pmatrix}0_n&I_n\\-I_n&0_n\end{pmatrix}\in M_{2n}(\mathbb R),$$
   whose blocks are $n\times n$.

derivative ([[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]]) gives
$d\lambda_U=\sum_i dp_i\wedge dq^i=-\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$. When $U$ is an induced chart domain of a

$\lambda_U$ and $\omega_U$ with the tautological one-form and the canonical cotangent two-form in
those coordinates; the present definition is the choice-free local coordinate model that the
canonical-calculus items of this page use.

$\omega_U=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ ([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]), and let

([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) and $J$ for the standard symplectic matrix. Then:

   $$X_H=J\nabla H=\bigl(H_{p_1},\dots,H_{p_n},-H_{q^1},\dots,-H_{q^n}\bigr);$$
2. an integral curve $t\mapsto(q(t),p(t))$ of $X_H$ satisfies Hamilton's equations

([[def-interval]]), let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty open set, and let

$$H:J\times U\times\mathbb R^n\longrightarrow\mathbb R$$

be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); write $p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ for

sense of [[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]]. Let
