([[def-metric-topology]]) and let $S:J'\times U'\times A'\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^3$; write
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ for the third variable.

$S$ **solves the Hamilton-Jacobi equation associated with $H$** on $J'\times U'\times A'$ if

$$S_t(t,q,\alpha)+H\bigl(t,\,q,\,S_q(t,q,\alpha)\bigr)=0\qquad\bigl((t,q,\alpha)\in J'\times U'\times A'\bigr),$$

([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]). $S$ is a

$$\det S_{q\alpha}(t_0,q_0,\alpha_0)\ne0,$$

$\partial^2S/\partial q^i\partial\alpha_j$, called the **mixed derivative**.

$$\Psi:O_q\times O_Q\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{2n},\qquad \Psi(q,Q):=\bigl(q,\ S_q(q,Q)\bigr),$$

whose derivative is the block matrix
$D\Psi(q,Q)=\begin{pmatrix}I_n&0\\ S_{qq}(q,Q)&S_{qQ}(q,Q)\end{pmatrix}$. A **generating function of
the first kind** is such an $S$; the **local map generated by $S$** is, on a neighbourhood of a point
$(q_*,Q_*)$, the $C^2$ map $C:(q,p)\mapsto(Q,P)$ defined by

$$p:=S_q(q,Q),\qquad P:=-S_Q(q,Q),$$

solved as follows: since $\det S_{qQ}\ne0$, the inverse function theorem
([[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]) makes $\Psi$ a local $C^2$ diffeomorphism, so
$p=S_q(q,Q)$ determines a $C^2$ local inverse $Q=Q(q,p)$ on a neighbourhood of
$\Psi(q_*,Q_*)$; then $C(q,p):=(Q(q,p),-S_Q(q,Q(q,p)))$.

**Second-kind data.** Let $O_q,O_P\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty open sets and let

**generating function of the second kind** is such an $S$; the **local map generated by $S$** is,
near a point $(q_*,P_*)$, the $C^2$ map $C:(q,p)\mapsto(Q,P)$ defined by

$$p:=S_q(q,P),\qquad Q:=S_P(q,P),$$

where again the relation $p=S_q(q,P)$ is solved locally for $P=P(q,p)$ by the inverse function
theorem applied to $(q,P)\mapsto(q,S_q(q,P))$, whose derivative is
$\begin{pmatrix}I_n&0\\ S_{qq}&S_{qP}\end{pmatrix}$.

**Recorded identities.** Wherever $S$ is of the first kind, the identity
$p\,dq-P\,dQ=dS$ holds; wherever $S$ is of the second kind, the identity $p\,dq+Q\,dP=dS$ holds,
both as identities of smooth one-forms on the $(q,Q)$- resp. $(q,P)$-space with $p,P,Q$ read as the
displayed functions ([[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]). The mixed-derivative hypotheses
$\det S_{qQ}\ne0$ resp. $\det S_{qP}\ne0$ are part of the data.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ be phase domains with standard two-forms $\omega_U$,
$\omega_V$ and the same matrix $J$ ([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]), and
let $C:U\to V$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Then:

1. $C^*\omega_V=\omega_U$ if and only if $DC(z)^{\mathsf T}J\,DC(z)=J$ for every $z\in U$;
2. if $C$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto $V$ and $C^*\omega_V=\omega_U$, then $C$ is a local
   symplectomorphism (equivalently a local canonical transformation,
   [[def-symplectomorphism-local-symplectomorphism-and-symplectic-embedding]],
   [[def-canonical-transformation]]) and $|\det DC(z)|=1$ for every $z\in U$;
3. if in addition $H\in C^2(V)$ and $C:U\to V$ is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism with $C^*\omega_V=\omega_U$,
   then $H\circ C\in C^2(U)$ and
   $$DC(z)\,X_{H\circ C}(z)=X_H\bigl(C(z)\bigr)\qquad(z\in U).$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U$ be a phase domain with canonical one-form $\lambda_U$, standard two-form
$\omega_U=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ and matrix $J=\begin{pmatrix}0_n&I_n\\-I_n&0_n\end{pmatrix}$
([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]). For a point $z\in U$ write
$\omega_z:=(\omega_U)_z$. Then:

1. $\omega_U$ is closed: $d\omega_U=0$;
2. for all $v,w\in\mathbb R^{2n}$, written in the coordinate frame as $v=(a,b)$ and $w=(c,d)$ with
   $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb R^n$, one has
   $$\omega_z(v,w)=v^{\mathsf T}J\,w=a\cdot d-b\cdot c ;$$
3. for every $v=(a,b)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n$ the contraction is the covector
   $$\iota_v\omega_z=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,dp_i-\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\,dq^i ;$$
4. $J^{\mathsf T}=-J$, $J^2=-I_{2n}$, and $J$ is invertible with $J^{-1}=J^{\mathsf T}=-J$;
5. consequently $v\mapsto\iota_v\omega_z$ is a linear isomorphism $\mathbb R^{2n}\to(\mathbb R^{2n})^*$,
   so $\omega_U$ is nondegenerate at every point and $(U,\omega_U)$ is a symplectic manifold.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

$q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]), let
$C:=\mathbb T\times\mathbb R$ be the cylinder, and identify $C$ with the quotient of $\mathbb R^2$

$\pi:\mathbb R^2\to C$ ([[def-quotient-topology]]); assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ where the cited

$\pi^*\omega_C=d\theta\wedge dI$ and $\pi^*\lambda_C=I\,d\theta$; while $d\theta$ descends to a

$\Phi(\theta,I)=(\theta,I+a)$. Then:

1. $\Phi$ is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism, $\Phi^*\omega_C=\omega_C$, and
   $\Phi^*\lambda_C=\lambda_C+a\,d\theta_C$;
2. $a\,d\theta_C$ is closed but not exact: there is no $C^1$ function $W:C\to\mathbb R$ with

3. for every point of $C$ there is a neighbourhood on which $\Phi$ is generated by the second-kind
   generating function $S(\theta,P)=\theta P-a\theta$, but there is no $C^1$ function
   $S:(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ whose generated map is $\Phi$; the local
   generating functions do not glue to a global one.

where $S_{qQ}(q,Q)$ is the $n\times n$ matrix with entries
$\partial^2 S/\partial q^i\partial Q^j(q,Q)$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]). Identify $O_q\times O_Q$ with the phase-domain coordinates
$(q,Q)$ of $\mathbb R^{2n}$ ([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]) and form the
$C^2$ map

$$\Psi:O_q\times O_Q\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{2n},\qquad \Psi(q,Q):=\bigl(q,\ S_q(q,Q)\bigr),$$

whose derivative is the block matrix
$D\Psi(q,Q)=\begin{pmatrix}I_n&0\\ S_{qq}(q,Q)&S_{qQ}(q,Q)\end{pmatrix}$. A **generating function of
the first kind** is such an $S$; the **local map generated by $S$** is, on a neighbourhood of a point

([[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]) makes $\Psi$ a local $C^2$ diffeomorphism, so

**generating function of the second kind** is such an $S$; the **local map generated by $S$** is,
near a point $(q_*,P_*)$, the $C^2$ map $C:(q,p)\mapsto(Q,P)$ defined by

$$p:=S_q(q,P),\qquad Q:=S_P(q,P),$$

where again the relation $p=S_q(q,P)$ is solved locally for $P=P(q,p)$ by the inverse function
theorem applied to $(q,P)\mapsto(q,S_q(q,P))$, whose derivative is
$\begin{pmatrix}I_n&0\\ S_{qq}&S_{qP}\end{pmatrix}$.

**Recorded identities.** Wherever $S$ is of the first kind, the identity
$p\,dq-P\,dQ=dS$ holds; wherever $S$ is of the second kind, the identity $p\,dq+Q\,dP=dS$ holds,
both as identities of smooth one-forms on the $(q,Q)$- resp. $(q,P)$-space with $p,P,Q$ read as the
displayed functions ([[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]). The mixed-derivative hypotheses
$\det S_{qQ}\ne0$ resp. $\det S_{qP}\ne0$ are part of the data.

derivations.claim: Clause 1 is [F1] specialised to $a=1$: $\Phi^*\lambda_C=\lambda_C+d\theta_C$ and $\Phi^*\omega_C=\omega_C$; clause 2 is the same proposition's non-exactness statement, whose proof integrates $d\theta_C$ along $\gamma$ to $1$.

Clause 3: on the chart $\theta\in(0,1)$ the derivatives of [F2] satisfy the second-kind relations $p=S_\theta=P-1$ and $Q=S_P=\theta$ with $S_{\theta P}=1\ne0$; the generated map is $(\theta,I)\mapsto(\theta,I+1)$, which is the shift, so $S$ generates $\Phi$ on the chart. Globally, [[prop-cm-cylinder-shift-has-no-global-generating-function]] clause 3 (with $a=1$) excludes any global $C^1$ generating function: a $1$-periodic lift $\hat S$ would satisfy $\hat S_P=\theta+m$ for a constant integer $m$ and $\hat S_\theta=P-1$, hence $\hat S(\theta,P)=\theta P+mP+c(\theta)$ with $c'=-1$, so $c(1)-c(0)=-1\ne0$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus, contradicting the periodicity $c(1)=c(0)$.

boundaries.reason: The shift is fixed at a=1 on the nonempty cylinder T times R, and the loop pi(t,0) has a specified parameter interval [0,1].
The fixed shift amount is one, never zero. The nonzero loop integral in step 1.1 is the stated obstruction to exactness.

boundaries.evidence: This example is exactly a single angular/action pair, with S_thetaP=1 and the scalar shift P=I+1 in step 2.1.
The local generating functions remain regular, but step 1.1 imports the integral-one obstruction to a global primitive; topology is the obstruction rather than a singular derivative.

The Example specifies the closed loop pi(t,0), t in [0,1], with equal projected endpoints and integral one; step 1.1 imports that obstruction. The local generating chart theta in (0,1) excludes its identified endpoints.

boundaries.reason: The example introduces no new choice: its cylinder and forms are supplied by the proposition, which explicitly records AC_omega for the torus. Its local S(theta,P)=theta P-theta is explicit.
The three clauses compute the fixed unit shift, a loop integral and one local generator; there is no biconditional statement.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U$ be a phase domain with standard two-form
$\omega_U=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ ([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]), and let
$H:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Write
$\nabla H=(H_{q^1},\dots,H_{q^n},H_{p_1},\dots,H_{p_n})$ for the Euclidean gradient
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) and $J$ for the standard symplectic matrix. Then:

1. there is exactly one $C^1$ vector field $X_H$ on $U$ with $\iota_{X_H}\omega_U=dH$, and it is
   $$X_H=J\nabla H=\bigl(H_{p_1},\dots,H_{p_n},-H_{q^1},\dots,-H_{q^n}\bigr);$$
2. an integral curve $t\mapsto(q(t),p(t))$ of $X_H$ satisfies Hamilton's equations
   $$\dot q^i=H_{p_i}(q,p),\qquad \dot p_i=-H_{q^i}(q,p)\qquad(i=1,\dots,n);$$
3. for $f,g\in C^2(U)$ the Poisson bracket
   $\{f,g\}:=\omega_U(X_f,X_g)$ ([[def-poisson-bracket-on-a-symplectic-manifold]]) is
   $$\{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\,\nabla g=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(f_{q^i}g_{p_i}-f_{p_i}g_{q^i}\bigr),$$
   hence $\{f,g\}=-\{g,f\}$, and $\{f,g\}$ is $C^1$ on $U$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U$ be a phase domain with standard two-form $\omega_U$ and matrix $J$, let
$H\in C^2(U)$, and let $\Phi$ be the local flow of the Hamiltonian field
$X_H=J\nabla H$ ([[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]],
[[def-cm-local-flow-of-an-autonomous-system]]). Let $z_0\in U$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be the open
interval of times $t$ with $(t,z_0)$ in the flow domain, and for $t\in I$ put

$$Y(t):=D_z\Phi_t(z_0)\in M_{2n}(\mathbb R).$$

Then $t\mapsto Y(t)$ is of class $C^1$ on $I$ and, for every $t\in I$:

1. (variational equation) $Y'(t)=J\,\mathrm{Hess}\,H(\Phi_t(z_0))\,Y(t)$ and $Y(0)=I_{2n}$;
2. (canonical matrix identity) $Y(t)^{\mathsf T}J\,Y(t)=J$;
3. (unit determinant) $\det Y(t)=1$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U$ be a phase domain with canonical one-form $\lambda_U$, standard two-form
$\omega_U=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ and matrix $J=\begin{pmatrix}0_n&I_n\\-I_n&0_n\end{pmatrix}$
([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]). For a point $z\in U$ write
$\omega_z:=(\omega_U)_z$. Then:

1. $\omega_U$ is closed: $d\omega_U=0$;
2. for all $v,w\in\mathbb R^{2n}$, written in the coordinate frame as $v=(a,b)$ and $w=(c,d)$ with
   $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb R^n$, one has
   $$\omega_z(v,w)=v^{\mathsf T}J\,w=a\cdot d-b\cdot c ;$$
3. for every $v=(a,b)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n$ the contraction is the covector
   $$\iota_v\omega_z=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,dp_i-\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\,dq^i ;$$
4. $J^{\mathsf T}=-J$, $J^2=-I_{2n}$, and $J$ is invertible with $J^{-1}=J^{\mathsf T}=-J$;
5. consequently $v\mapsto\iota_v\omega_z$ is a linear isomorphism $\mathbb R^{2n}\to(\mathbb R^{2n})^*$,
   so $\omega_U$ is nondegenerate at every point and $(U,\omega_U)$ is a symplectic manifold.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

derivations.claim: Clause 1: by [F1] the field is $X_H=(p,-q)$ and the flow solves the linear system; the displayed $\Phi_t$ satisfies $\Phi_0=\mathrm{id}$ and, by [F2], its derivatives are $q'=p(t)$ and $p'=-q(t)$, so by uniqueness it is the flow, defined for all real $t$.

Clause 2: differentiating $Y(t)$ entrywise gives $Y'(t)=\begin{pmatrix}-\sin t&\cos t\\-\cos t&-\sin t\end{pmatrix}$, while $J\,\mathrm{Hess}\,H\,Y=JY=\begin{pmatrix}-\sin t&\cos t\\-\cos t&-\sin t\end{pmatrix}$; thus $Y'=JY$ with $Y(0)=I_2$.
The orthogonality of $Y(t)$ gives $Y^{\mathsf T}JY=J$ by direct multiplication, and $\det Y=\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1$; hence both conclusions of [F3] hold explicitly for this flow.

boundaries.reason: The domain is the whole nonempty phase plane R² and H=(p squared+q squared)/2 is a single fixed Hamiltonian.

boundaries.evidence: At q=p=0, step 1.1 gives the stationary zero orbit, while the derivative matrix in step 1.2 remains the same rotation matrix with determinant one.
n=1 is explicit, and step 1.2 verifies the complete two by two variational matrix directly.

boundaries.reason: The Hessian is I_2 and the displayed Y is orthogonal for every t; no vanishing determinant occurs in step 2.1.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.2 verifies Y(0)=I_2, and step 2.1 gives its canonical identity for all real t, including the initial time.

boundaries.reason: The oscillator flow and derivative are explicit sine/cosine matrices; their computation in steps 1.1–1.2 requires no arbitrary solution selection.
The Example computes a Hamiltonian flow derivative and checks three identities; it does not assert an equivalence classifying all orthogonal flows.
It does not reconstruct the oscillator Hamiltonian from an arbitrary determinant-one matrix; the given H determines Y.
